BACK TO ALL ARTICLES

# What is the Queensland Media Club?

[GOVERNMENT](https://www.streem.com.au/blog/tag/government)

[The Queensland Media Club](https://www.threeplus.com.au/our-sponsors/) (QMC) is the official political, business and media forum of the Queensland Parliament Media Gallery, managed by [Three Plus](https://www.threeplus.com.au/) , a full ‑ service communications consultancy. Insightful, colourful and entertaining, the QMC stands as one of Australia’s most influential forums for business leaders and decision-makers. The club hosts six business networking lunches each year, drawing more than 300 guests on average. The audience becomes part of breaking news as announcements are made, journalists ask hard questions and speakers’ insights become headlines just minutes later. QLD Media Club Event March 2025 with Jim Chalmers  
## **What They Do** At every event, the Queensland Media Club creates a unique setting where breaking news meets live conversation.
As guests gather for the networking lunches, they experience firsthand the rapid pace at which major announcements and discussions unfold. The club offers an opportunity for direct engagement with political and business decision-makers. Recent events have covered topics as diverse as federal budget previews, election debates, policy announcements and strategic discussions about Queensland and Australia’s future. Speakers have included Treasurer Jim Chalmers, State Premiers, MP’s, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. ## **Who Should Attend** The Queensland Media Club is ideal for: * Corporate leaders and executives **:** Gain valuable insights from discussions that shape policy and business strategy. The networking opportunities and direct access to influential speakers help attendees stay ahead of critical trends.
* Communications professionals: QM C events offer a unique front-row seat to how major news and policy announcements are reported and discussed in real time.
Attendees witness the evolution of messaging strategies, helping them refine their approach to public relations, crisis management and stakeholder engagement.
  
  
## **A Connection with Streem** As a proud Club Partner of the Queensland Media Club, Streem shares the club’s commitment to making news more accessible and impactful. Much like QMC creates a unique, accessible environment for direct engagement with top decision-makers, we’re committed to making media and news more accessible through our platform, so every stakeholder can easily tap into accurate, up-to-the-minute information. ## **Join the Conversation** Become part of a community where ideas, discussion and dynamic engagement help shape the future of media, politics and business in Australia. To find out more, visit the [Queensland Media Club’s website](https://www.threeplus.com.au/our-sponsors/) or [subscribe to the QMC’s distribution list](https://bit.ly/QMC-Subscribe) to be the first to receive event updates.

The **2023 Australian Indigenous Voice referendum** was a constitutional referendum held on 14 October 2023 in which the proposed Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Voice was rejected. Voters were asked to approve an alteration to the Australian Constitution that would recognise Indigenous Australians in the document through [prescribing](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/prescribe "wiktionary:prescribe") a body called the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Voice that would have been able to make representations to Federal Parliament and the executive government on "matters relating to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples". [[ 1 ]]()

The proposal was rejected nationally and by a majority in every state, thus failing to secure the double majority required for amendment by section 128 of the constitution . The Australian Capital Territory was the only state or territory with a majority of "yes" votes.
Analysis of surveys following the referendum identified the main reasons why the majority of Australians voted no was a scepticism of granting rights to some Australians that are not held by others and an aversion to constitutional change.

Detailed analysis of the 2023 Voice to Parliament Referendum and related social and political attitudes

Detailed analysis of the 2023 Voice to Parliament Referendum and related social and political attitudes

**Author/editor:** Biddle,N, Gray, M, McAllister, I & Qvortrup, M

**Year published:** 2023

## Abstract
On the 14th of October 2023, Australians voted on a proposal ‘To alter the Constitution to recognise the First Peoples of Australia by establishing an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Voice.’ Only 39.9 per cent of legal votes were in favour of this change, and there was not a majority or close to a majority in any of the six Australian States (there was a majority, however, in the Australian Capital Territory). In order to support an informed discussion about the referendum and its aftermath, the Australian National University collected a detailed survey immediately following the referendum (the October 2023 Australian Constitutional Referendum Study (ACRS)/ANUpoll) from a broadly representative sample of over 4,000 adult Australians. The survey data is available from the Australian Data Archive (doi:10.26193/13NPGQ).

There is no evidence in the data to suggest that Australians are against the idea of constitutional recognition in general.
Of those who were willing to give an opinion as to what their vote would have been if the referendum was just about recognition those who would vote yes outnumber those who would vote no by a margin of almost five-to-one. The vote also did not signal a lack of support for reconciliation, for the importance of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders having a voice/say in matters that affect them, truth-telling processes, or for a lack of pride in First Nations cultures. All of these notions were supported in our survey by around eight-in-ten Australians, or even more. We did find, however, that compared to start of the year, Australians are far less satisfied with democracy, less confident in the government, less satisfied with the direction of the country, and less satisfied with their own life.

Our survey data tells us a few things about who was more or less likely to vote yes.
